title: Children of the resurrection (Luke 20:20–40)
hook: trick questions about taxes and the dead: for all live to him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beloved son, sent last of all, and the stone the builders rejected. Your line was they will respect my son. Who got a second hearing from you? Day five hundred seventy-three.

A trick question is built so that every answer loses. Ask a politician whether they've stopped wasting money and watch them squirm. Luke says the leaders now send spies who pretend to be sincere, with a question like that. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Say yes, and the crowd hears a man who bows to Rome. Say no, and Rome hears a rebel. Jesus asks for a coin and asks whose picture is on it. Caesar's. Then, in the King James Bible: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's." They go quiet. And then a second group arrives with a second trap, this one about the dead.

The second group are Sadducees, and Luke tells us they deny that there is any resurrection. So they spin a story to make the idea look ridiculous. Moses taught that if a man dies without children, his brother should marry the widow. Seven brothers, one after another, marry the same woman, and each one dies. In the resurrection, whose wife will she be? Jesus doesn't laugh at them. He says the life to come isn't a copy of this one. People there don't marry, because they can't die any more. They are, in the King James words, "the children of God, being the children of the resurrection." That phrase is a Hebrew way of speaking. A child of something is someone who belongs to it, whose life is shaped by it. Then Jesus goes back to Moses himself, to the burning bush, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, long after all three had died. Not the God they used to have. Their God, now. And then the line that is today's carry: "For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him." One more detail. In this argument Jesus stands on the same side as the Pharisees, who also taught the resurrection. And Luke says some of the scribes answered, "Master, thou hast well said." After that, nobody dares ask him anything. At funerals, some Christians hear in all live to him a promise about the people they've lost: that they are not gone from God, even when they are gone from us.
screen: `THE GOD OF ABRAHAM, ISAAC AND JACOB.`
then, large: `FOR ALL LIVE UNTO HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who died in hope. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you've lost. A grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even a pet if that's where your heart goes. Let their face come, or their voice, or their hands. You don't have to feel anything big. Just let them be near for a minute. If you pray, you can say their name to God and Jesus's words with it: all live unto him. If you don't, simply hold them with gratitude, and with whatever hope you have. The bell holds the time.
Children of the resurrection. Jesus's name for those who rise: people who belong to the life that doesn't die, and so belong to God.
Your line: all live to him. Today, say the name of someone you've lost out loud, to a friend or just to the room, and tell one small story about them. Day five hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Some churches read Jesus's answer to the Sadducees at funerals or on All Souls' Day, and some remember their dead by name in worship.

original.note: Greek: sons of the resurrection. a Semitic idiom: a 'son of' something belongs to it or shares its nature.

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle about marriage in heaven.
what it means: a trap meant to mock the resurrection, answered with the God of the living, for whom all live.
what a scholar hears: 'children of the resurrection' is a Semitic idiom of belonging, and on this point Jesus sides with the Pharisees against the Sadducees.

notes: Pharisees taught the resurrection and Sadducees denied it (Luke 20:27; Acts 23:8). Confirm the brief framing is fair to both.
'Children of' as a Semitic idiom of belonging: standard commentary. Confirm.
Levirate marriage summarized from Deuteronomy 25:5–6. Confirm.
Practice invites remembering the dead; for some traditions, praying for the dead is customary and for others it is not. The practice is phrased so either can do it.
